analysis.one_liner: Slaps a 75% tax on bonuses paid by banks, insurers, hedge funds, and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a 75% excise tax, paid by the employer, on any bonus paid to workers at banks, insurers, hedge funds, securities dealers, financial advisers, and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, for five years after enactment. The tax could not be deducted from corporate income taxes. Sponsors argued that public bailouts and cheap federal support had propped up the financial industry while banks used profits for bonuses instead of rebuilding their capital and lending.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public, in two ways. First, the tax would capture most of the value of large bonuses paid by financial firms during the recovery and return it to the Treasury, on the theory that public subsidies had made those profits possible. Second, by making bonuses far more expensive, it would push financial firms to use earnings to strengthen their balance sheets and restore lending to businesses and households instead.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and households waiting for restored credit

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 75% tax, paid by the employer rather than the employee, on any bonus paid for services at Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, any financial institution, insurance company, hedge fund, financial adviser, securities broker or dealer, or any lending or finance business [S3].
The tax applies for five years after enactment and applies to bonuses paid after the bill's enactment date [S3].

The bill states as findings that banks used public subsidies in the form of cost-free access to capital, low-cost federal loans and guarantees, and purchases of troubled assets, and that using profits for bonuses rather than recapitalization delayed recovery of both the banks and the real economy [S3].
The tax is not deductible for corporate tax purposes, so firms could not offset it against their income taxes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms and their bonus recipients. The tax is levied on the company paying the bonus, and because it is not deductible, the full cost stays with the firm. It would apply to every bonus at covered firms, not only outsized executive payouts, so rank-and-file employees in banking and insurance who receive standard bonuses would also be affected.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks, insurers, hedge funds, and their employees

drawbacks.text: The 75% tax applies to any bonus at a covered firm, not just large executive payouts, so a modest year-end bonus at a regional bank or insurance company would be hit by the same 75% levy as a seven-figure Wall Street payout [S3].

Because the tax is set as a flat percentage on all bonuses for five years, firms would have strong incentives to restructure pay into salaries, deferred compensation, or other forms that avoid the definition of a bonus, and to route work through entities outside the covered categories [S3].

Critics of bonus taxes generally argue that taxing compensation does not itself fix bank balance sheets; the bill's own findings concede that enhanced capital adequacy, not compensation policy alone, is what restores lending, and a compensation tax is a blunt instrument for that goal [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is coherent: after a crisis in which public money and federal guarantees kept financial firms alive, taxing outsized bonus pools and pushing firms toward recapitalization addresses a real grievance. But the bill as written is a blunt tool. It taxes all bonuses equally at covered firms, reaches ordinary employees alongside executives, and gives firms predictable ways to restructure around it. A better-designed version would have targeted very large bonuses or firms still holding federal support. The tradeoff is real but the design is rough.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on January 12, 2010, with five original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
Eight House Democrats in total cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral to Ways and Means [S5].
The bill never advanced past committee and received no vote in either chamber before the 111th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms kept the ability to pay bonuses free of any special tax, and their employees' bonuses remained untaxed by the levy. No other party gained from the bill's death, since it simply disappeared in committee. Financial firms are better off than they would have been under the bill; taxpayers and households waiting for restored bank lending gained nothing from the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms that avoided the bonus tax
